Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-07 15:00 UTC
Duration: 28 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Tom Alvarez (Redwood SE), Sarah Li (Cascade SRE), Mike Nguyen (Eng Mgr), Priya Patel (Security), Aaron Cole (Platform)

Summary: quick follow-up from escalation on 2027-09-03 where customer-facing requests saw elevated 5xx and tail latency spikes. Focus: root-cause confirmation, short-term mitigations, rollout plan for autoscaler + KV cache fixes, and security/compliance sign-offs.

Topics: incident timeline, KV cache behavior under burst, autoscaler and slot allocation, fallback model strategy, observability gaps, SOC2 / KMS questions, next steps.

Action items (recorded): see metadata action_items above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for hopping on uh we wanted to run through the postmortem follow up from last friday, it's mostly Tom + me to walk through the root cause and proposed mitigations, then we'll sync on next steps, Sarah can you quickly confirm the customer impact?
[00:22] Sarah Li: yeah so on 09/03 around 14:12 UTC our frontend started seeing a 10-15% increase in 5xx and some requests hit 1.2s tail latency, um the majority were generation calls, not embeddings, and our incident page shows spikes aligned to a job that re-ran a dataset processing flow, so definitely a bursty prefix pattern, and we put the service into read-only for about 18 minutes while we ramped capacity.
[00:48] Tom Alvarez: right and from Redwood's traces the runtime saw a sudden KV cache miss storm and a backpressure cascade where batching queues grew, some requests timed out, which caused retries from the client and amplified the load -- essentially a feedback loop. there were also a couple of model swaps during the incident which didn't help, those were manual fallbacks.
[01:15] Mike Nguyen: when you say KV cache miss storm, are we talking about prefix cache misses or a totally cold cache because of a restart? I remember we had a pod flapping event earlier.
[01:32] Tom Alvarez: good question, so the evidence points to a mix: one control-plane reschedule caused a small number of pods to restart (we flagged those) but the dominant signal was workload-driven: a large batch of unique prompts invalidated the prefix/KV cache locality, so we saw simultaneous KV loads across nodes which spiked memory and I/O. that increased token generation latency and exhausted some GPU inference slots.
[02:01] Priya Patel: just to flag from security, the customer is asking for proof that logs we share don't expose PII and that the KMS keys used for encrypted model artifacts haven't rotated unexpectedly. plus they want an audit trail for the autoscaler changes, is that something Redwood can provide?
[02:21] Maya Chen: yes, Priya, we'll share filtered logs with PII redaction and a KMS rotation history. i've got the SOC2 report link and we can provide the audit log export for the control plane changes — i'll send those after this call.
[02:40] Aaron Cole: one thing we noticed is the autoscaler thresholds are very conservative for bursty workloads; the scale-up window is like 90s which is too slow for these short spikes. can we tune that?
[02:56] Tom Alvarez: the default burst policy is indeed aimed at steady growth; we can propose a faster ramp policy for dedicated pools or increase warm pools. quick fix options: 1) reduce scale-up cooldown to 20-30s, 2) pre-warm extra slots for scheduled batch jobs, 3) enable a transient burst pool that can absorb short surges.
[03:22] Sarah Li: ok we can try pre-warming for the nightly jobs, but we also want a safety net so a bad job doesn't increase costs too much. is there a way to set a cost cap or fallback to a cheaper model when slots are saturated?
[03:40] Tom Alvarez: yes, fallback routing is supported — we can route to a quantized variant or a lower-capacity model when latency SLOs risk being violated. that keeps availability up while saving tokens. there is work to surface cost cap alerts in console, but we can implement routing policies quickly.
[03:59] Maya Chen: and we'll help build a canary for that behavior so it only triggers under test traffic first.
[04:10] Mike Nguyen: another root cause question: earlier logs show a spike in 'k.v. cache' io ops, but some of the stacktrace symbols are garbled in our export, is that a known transcriber issue or something else?
[04:26] Tom Alvarez: sometimes the trace names get truncated in our collector during heavy throughput, that's more of an observability edge case; we already have an internal ticket to increase buffer sizes on the trace exporter. i'll include that ticket id in the timeline.
[04:45] Sarah Li: also noticed some 502s from our edge which made us think it was upstream, that delayed our mitigation while debugging caches. can we add a synthetic monitor that hits the Redwood endpoint with typical prefixes so we can detect prefix-eviction problems earlier?
[05:03] Tom Alvarez: absolutely, synthetic checks per prefix/family are a good idea, we can share a small script + k6 profile.
[05:15] Priya Patel: on the compliance side, can you confirm that audit logs show who executed the manual fallback model swaps during the incident? we need to map actions to users for our internal audit.
[05:30] Maya Chen: yes we'll export the control plane audit logs and mask tokens, the log entries include user IDs and timestamps.
[05:40] Aaron Cole: in terms of longer-term reliability work what are the recommended infra changes from Redwood?
[05:49] Tom Alvarez: short list: faster autoscaler cooldowns for bursty workloads, transient burst pools, stronger KV cache eviction heuristics (pin hot prefixes), increase trace exporter buffers, and a canary routing policy for fallback models; medium-term: per-tenant prewarming and cost-aware routing that can automatically apply budget caps.
[06:18] Mike Nguyen: how risky is change number one? i.e., reducing cooldown to 20s, could that cause flapping?
[06:27] Tom Alvarez: risk is moderate, but we mitigate with rate-limited scale-down and a canary rollout. we can also implement a CPU/memory threshold check before adding GPUs so spurious signals don't cause flapping.
[06:45] Sarah Li: would be good to see a proposed canary plan and run it against our staging traffic.
[06:52] Maya Chen: we'll draft a canary runbook and share, Tom will own the staging tests.
[06:59] Tom Alvarez: for the KV cache itself we recommend two fixes: 1) pinning hot prefixes in memory for 24 hours, 2) introducing a lightweight lease so a single node loads a prefix and shares readiness — reduces thundering herd. both are low risk and can be rolled to staging in a week.
[07:25] Priya Patel: lease mechanism seems fine but does it introduce cross-node calls that could leak data? we need a security review.
[07:35] Tom Alvarez: no PII is exchanged, it's just cache meta coordination (prefix id + readiness bit). still we'll include design docs and threat model for Priya to review.
[07:49] Maya Chen: next on the list is observability: the team requested more granular latency percentiles and token-level cost attribution per route — we can enable additional metrics and dashboard tiles.
[08:04] Aaron Cole: please add alerts for sustained p95 > 800ms or >3% 5xx over 5 minutes. that would have caught this earlier.
[08:12] Tom Alvarez: will do. also we noticed some retry amplification from client libraries; one mitigation is to add jittered backoff recommendations and an idempotency key for generation requests.
[08:29] Mike Nguyen: do you have recommended client settings for nodejs sdk? our client uses default retry policy right now.
[08:36] Maya Chen: yes we'll send the recommended SDK config: retries=2, base backoff 200ms with jitter, and idempotency header X-Request-ID.
[08:47] Sarah Li: ok that should help. a separate ask from ops: can Redwood provide a small runbook snippet we can paste into our internal runbook to triage similar incidents?
[08:58] Maya Chen: yes, we'll include a triage checklist: identify prefix burst, check KV miss rate, check pod restarts, validate autoscaler metrics, and fallback routing status.
[09:12] Tom Alvarez: regarding the model swap that happened, the control plane UI allowed a manual swap mid-incident — we'll add a confirmation and secondary approval requirement for model swaps in production for customers who opt-in.
[09:28] Priya Patel: please make that opt-in configurable, we can't have accidental swaps during incidents.
[09:34] Maya Chen: agreed.
[09:38] Mike Nguyen: timeline-wise when can we expect the staging KV fixes and autoscaler tuning to be available for our team to test?
[09:45] Tom Alvarez: estimate: KV pin + lease in staging by 2027-09-13, autoscaler cooldown + burst pool config change in staging by 2027-09-11. we'll run a replay of the job that caused the burst and share results.
[10:02] Sarah Li: thanks, please also include a comparison of cost impact for the burst pool approach vs fallback routing so we can discuss with finance.
[10:12] Maya Chen: we'll include a cost delta spreadsheet with assumptions.
[10:18] Aaron Cole: one more thing — can you provide the exact control-plane audit entries for the people who performed the manual model fallback? our compliance team wants to reconcile actions with Slack messages.
[10:30] Maya Chen: yes we'll export that with PII redaction but preserving user ids.
[10:37] Priya Patel: on KMS, we need confirmation that key usage logs show no unexpected decrypts during the incident window.
[10:45] Tom Alvarez: we'll pull the KMS usage logs and include the 14:00-14:30 UTC window, annotate it with model loads.
[10:54] Mike Nguyen: ok, seems like a good plan. any objections to Redwood running the staging replay under an agreed maintenance window?
[11:05] Sarah Li: no objection, just a heads-up that we'll monitor cost and throttle if needed.
[11:12] Maya Chen: perfect, we'll follow the actions and send a consolidated follow up email with timelines and attachments.
[11:20] Tom Alvarez: i'll include the exporter traces, the synthetic check script, and the canary runbook.
[11:28] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, recap: Tom to run traces + staging replay, Maya to send security docs + SOC2 link, customer to share alert screenshots. follow-up meeting in two weeks unless we need an earlier sync.
[11:44] Mike Nguyen: thanks all.

Notes: transcript contains some automated transcription artifacts: 'k.v. cache' vs 'KV cache', occasional speaker mislabels. Links/attachments referenced: incident timeline link (to be shared), SOC2 report (link), cost delta spreadsheet (link), canary runbook (link).
